Measuring the distance to Supernova 1987A

Supernova 1987A. Determining distances in the Universe is one of the fundamental problems of astronomy. On 23 February 1987 a supernova visible to the naked eye appeared in the Large Magellanic Cloud. An accurate measurement of the distance to SN 1987A can be used to determine the distance to the Large Magellanic Cloud itself.

The first images of SN 1987A were taken with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. They show three circular nebulae surrounding the supernova, an inner one and two outer ones. We shall use only the inner one. All of these are shown in Figures 1 and 2. The ring lies too far from the supernova to be material ejected at the moment of the explosion. It is probably related to a nebula that had been created earlier, most likely from material that was blown away from the star by its stellar wind during the last millennia of its life. When a flash of ultraviolet radiation from SN 1987A reached the nebula, it began to glow. We shall assume that the ring is perfectly circular, but we see it inclined, and that is why it has the shape of an ellipse. If we did not see it inclined, all parts of the ring would "light up" at the same moment, when the ultraviolet radiation arrived from the supernova.

However, because we see it inclined, the part nearest to us glowed first (because of the finite speed of light), and then the light appeared to "move" along the ring, reaching the farthest point last. That is, although all parts of the ring began to glow simultaneously, we saw the nearer parts glow first. This is shown in Figure 3.

Since the gas continued to glow and began to fade slowly after the flash had passed, the brightness of the ring reached its maximum when the whole circumference was glowing.

Colour–Magnitude Diagrams of star clusters

In this exercise you will use photometric data from two star clusters to calculate some of the properties of these clusters. The data consist of photographs in two filters, the visual (V) and the blue (B). The difference of the brightness of a star in the blue and in the visual (B−V) is a good measure of the temperature of the star's photosphere (Figure 1). This difference is called the colour index.

Thus, a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram can be expressed in terms of luminosity and temperature or — equivalently — in terms of absolute magnitude and colour index (Figure 2).

Such a diagram, which uses apparent instead of absolute magnitudes, is the observational analogue of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and is called a Colour–Magnitude Diagram (CMD). Such diagrams are used in the study of star clusters (Figure 3).

This data analysis exercise concerns star clusters exclusively. It starts with some simple orientation questions, continues with the representation of the data in a CMD and ends with questions of interpretation of the data and calculations. The photometric data have undergone the initial processing and are given as relative magnitudes (that is, they have no physical meaning by themselves but are given relative to an — arbitrary — reference star). What is asked of you here is work that astronomy students and researchers working on a similar problem would do. [The photometric observations were kindly provided by Dr Ulrich Kolb.]

Task 4:

In this task you will calculate the distance of the cluster "Zeus". The intrinsic colour (colour index) of a star is determined by its spectral type. Nevertheless, the passage of light through the interstellar matter tends to "redden" every star (more blue is absorbed than other colours). This extinction depends on the amount of interstellar matter between the cluster and the Earth, so it is the same for all the stars of each cluster. The difference between the observed colour index and the intrinsic one is found empirically and is equal to 1/3 of the extinction index. The extinction index for the cluster Zeus is $\Delta = 0.78$.

The distance of a star of the cluster (and consequently of the cluster) is given by the relation
$$M = m + 5 - 5\log d - \Delta,$$
where $M$ and $m$ are the absolute and apparent magnitudes of the star and $d$ is measured in parsecs (pc). You will apply this relation to the magnitudes in the visual ($M_V$, $m_V$).

In the next step you will choose the appropriate star to apply this formula to. By definition, a star of spectral type A0 is one that has intrinsic colour index 0 (that is, its B and V magnitudes are equal). Consequently, a star of true spectral type A0 will appear on your diagram with colour index $\Delta/3$. The absolute visual magnitude of an A0 main-sequence star is $M_V = 0.7$.

(b) Use your estimate in (a) to calculate the distance of the cluster in pc.

(c) In (a) you have most probably identified a range of values of $m_V$ corresponding to spectral type A0. Use the maximum and the minimum value to calculate the corresponding distances (minimum and maximum, according to the error) of the cluster. Give your answer as follows: "the best estimate is … pc and the corresponding values of minimum and maximum distance are …" (e.g. suppose that the best estimate of the distance you found in question (b) is $d = 102$ pc; then the values of minimum and maximum distance would be 87 pc and 109 pc).

Cosmological model via SNIa

A type Ia supernova (SN Ia) is caused by the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf (WD) when the mass of the WD, which grows by accretion from a companion star, reaches the Chandrasekhar limit (about $1.4\,M_\odot$). The composition of the white dwarf determines the spectrum of the supernova (Figure 1). It is the absorption lines in this spectrum that characterize the supernova and distinguish it from supernovae of other types. Because the explosion happens as soon as the Chandrasekhar limit is exceeded, the luminosity of all SN Ia is (almost) the same. For this reason these supernovae are used as standard candles. Moreover, because of their luminosity they are visible at very large distances.

In this exercise you will use photometric data from 2 groups of SN Ia in order to calculate the expansion constant of the Universe locally, $H_0$, and to draw qualitative conclusions about the cosmological model that governs the Universe.

The luminosity of a supernova rises very rapidly, stays about constant at maximum for a few days and then declines slowly (Figure 2, left part). Of course, there are small differences between the light curves of these supernovae (e.g. the brighter ones decline more slowly). Careful analysis allows us to take such peculiarities into account and arrive at a light curve that is representative of SN Ia, the reference curve (Figure 2, right part). Thus the light curve of every newly appearing SN Ia can be compared with the reference curve and give us a measurement of the distance of the source (luminosity distance).

In addition, from the absorption lines of the spectrum we calculate the redshift $z$:
$$z = \frac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0} \qquad \text{[Equation 1]}$$
where $\lambda_0$ is the wavelength of the absorption line and $\lambda$ the wavelength at which it is observed in the supernova in question.

Hubble showed that galaxies recede from us with speeds proportional to their distance. This is interpreted as an expansion of the Universe, and for sources near us
$$v = H_0\, d \qquad \text{[Equation 2]}$$
where $d$ is the distance of the source, $H_0$ is a constant (the Hubble constant) and $v$ is the recession speed of the source, which is determined from the redshift, $v/c = (\lambda - \lambda_0)/\lambda_0$, and which, using Equation 1, can be expressed as
$$v = z\,c \qquad \text{[Equation 3]}$$
where $c$ is the speed of light.

By convention the Hubble constant $H_0$ is measured in km/s/Mpc. SN Ia have absolute visual magnitude at maximum light $M = -19.0 \pm 0.4$. The apparent magnitude is given by
$$m - M = 5\log d - 5 \qquad \text{[Equation 4]}$$
where $d$ is measured in pc.

At the beginning of 2016 the first detection of gravitational waves by the LIGO team was announced. We all had the unique luck to live through this historic event. The picture (and our understanding) of the Universe will change drastically during your lifetime!

Gravitational waves are not like electromagnetic waves. They change spacetime, "stretching" it a little in one direction while shrinking it in the perpendicular one (and then the other way round), periodically. This periodic change of the fabric of spacetime is extremely small, but it can (now) be measured. For example, a distance of one metre will be stretched/shrunk by $10^{-22}$ m! So we measure the strength of gravitational waves as the fraction of "stretching" (strain) of spacetime relative to its dimensions in the absence of a gravitational wave. Consequently, the quantity strain is dimensionless.

As the black holes revolve around each other, they gradually lose energy and angular momentum, so that they come ever closer to each other. This leads to their finally falling into each other's arms. The loss of this energy creates the gravitational waves that we detect. Figure 1 shows the waveform of the gravitational-wave signal of the source GW151226.

The equations that follow are approximate, but quite accurate before the last orbits shortly before the merger. In these equations we measure time — by convention and for convenience — from the moment of the merger (that is, of the creation of the large black hole). Consequently, events before the merger appear at negative times (a countdown!).

In one orbital period $P_\mathrm{orb}$, the system produces two periods $P_\mathrm{GW}$ of the gravitational wave:
$$P_\mathrm{orb} = 2P_\mathrm{GW} \qquad \text{(Equation 1)}$$
The orbital period changes with time according to the relation
$$P_\mathrm{orb}(t) = \left(P_0^{8/3} - \frac{8}{3}kt\right)^{3/8} \qquad \text{(Equation 2)}$$
where $P_0$ is the period exactly before the merger and $k$ is the constant
$$k = \frac{96}{5c^5}(2\pi)^{8/3}\left(G\widetilde{M}\right)^{5/3} \qquad \text{(Equation 3)}$$
and $\widetilde{M}$ is called the "chirp mass" (if we convert the gravitational signal into sound, it resembles a chirp, whose timbre depends on this quantity) and is given by the following combination of the masses $M_1$ and $M_2$ of the 2 black holes:
$$\widetilde{M} = (M_1 M_2)^{3/5}(M_1 + M_2)^{-1/5} \qquad \text{(Equation 4)}$$
